output.formulary_status: Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate, lacosamide, lorazepam and midazolam IV: formulary.
interactions: Levetiracetam in end-stage renal disease: renally cleared, and about half of the body load is removed by a 4-hour hemodialysis; loading dose unchanged, maintenance 500-1000 mg once daily with a 250-500 mg supplement after each dialysis

Fosphenytoin in end-stage renal disease: uremia and low albumin reduce protein binding, so total phenytoin levels underestimate the free level; the prodrug releases phosphate during conversion; IV loading risks hypotension and conduction block
Lacosamide in end-stage renal disease: maximum 300 mg/day maintenance, removed by hemodialysis with a supplement after dialysis; dose-dependent PR prolongation
Midazolam in renal failure: its active glucuronide metabolite accumulates; prolonged sedation
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + amlodipine: enzyme induction lowers amlodipine exposure
Insulin glargine and lispro in end-stage renal disease: reduced insulin clearance; risk of hypoglycemia with poor intake
Sevelamer: binds some oral drugs given at the same time; no interaction with IV antiseizure drugs
output.proposed: Antiseizure options (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate, lacosamide, lorazepam, midazolam) in end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, against sevelamer, epoetin, amlodipine and insulin
output.summary: Levetiracetam and lacosamide need renal maintenance dosing and post-dialysis supplements. Fosphenytoin has altered protein binding in uremia, adds a phosphate load and can block conduction. Midazolam metabolites accumulate in renal failure.
warnings: Lorazepam: single doses need no renal adjustment; monitor respiration
Magnesium- and phosphate-containing products accumulate in end-stage renal disease

output.query: Antiseizure drug dosing in end-stage renal disease and status epilepticus treatment

results.finding: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine [Glauser_2016].
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective as second-line agents in ESETT [ESETT_2019].
Levetiracetam is cleared by the kidneys and removed by hemodialysis, so maintenance doses are reduced and supplemented after dialysis, while loading doses are unchanged.
In uremia, phenytoin protein binding falls, so free rather than total levels guide dosing.

output.summary: Status epilepticus is treated with a benzodiazepine and then one of three equally effective second-line drugs [Glauser_2016; ESETT_2019]; renally cleared antiseizure drugs need maintenance adjustment and post-dialysis supplements in end-stage renal disease.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: BUN 142 and creatinine 14.8; potassium 6.8; calcium 6.8 with albumin 3.4; phosphate 8.4; sodium 128; bicarbonate 12 with pH 7.15; magnesium 2.9; glucose 142
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; after a missed dialysis, potassium, calcium and acidosis also decide the urgency of dialysis, and glucose matters on insulin with poor intake [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: Potassium 6.8 after a missed dialysis can cause conduction block and arrhythmia; ECG changes make membrane stabilization urgent and bear on a conduction-active ASM [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP; uremic platelet dysfunction raises the risk of subdural hematoma [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: Levetiracetam is renally cleared and removed by dialysis, and fosphenytoin binding and phosphate load change in uremia, which decides the second-line ASM and its maintenance [ESETT_2019].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not use renally cleared ASMs at standard maintenance doses.
Do not give IV magnesium or phosphate-containing products: magnesium is 2.9 and phosphate 8.4 in end-stage renal disease.
Do not give gadolinium for the MRI unless it is essential: end-stage renal disease.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].
Stabilize the myocardium for hyperkalemia with ECG changes: IV calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL over 5 to 10 minutes, repeated if the ECG changes persist, which also treats the hypocalcemia.
Shift potassium with IV regular insulin (5 units in end-stage renal disease to limit hypoglycemia) with 25 g dextrose, and check glucose hourly.

Arrange emergency hemodialysis with nephrology as the definitive treatment of uremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis and volume overload; with BUN 142, make the first session gentle (short, low blood flow) to avoid dialysis disequilibrium.

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), with the load unchanged and renal maintenance dosing with a supplement after each dialysis, and avoid fosphenytoin because its binding is altered in uremia, it adds a phosphate load, and loading risks conduction block on this ECG [ESETT_2019].
Lower the blood pressure of 198/118 in a controlled way (about 25% over the first hours) with IV labetalol or nicardipine, alongside fluid removal by dialysis.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
An ambulatory Holter adds nothing: the hyperkalemic conduction changes are on the 12-lead ECG, and inpatient telemetry is part of management.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.
Uremia with severe metabolic derangement explains the presentation without fever or meningism; LP is not indicated initially.

accepted: Uremic status epilepticus from missed hemodialysis with severe metabolic derangement (BUN 142, K 6.8, Ca 6.8, Na 128) in ESRD

differential.key_features: Calcium 6.8 (about 7.3 corrected for albumin 3.4) can provoke seizures and contributes, but it is part of the uremic derangement with BUN 142; hyperkalemia causes conduction changes, not seizures
BP 198/118 raises it, but MRI shows no parieto-occipital vasogenic edema
Uremia causes platelet dysfunction, but CT shows no hemorrhage or subdural collection

differential.diagnosis: Hypoglycemia from insulin with reduced renal clearance
differential.key_features: Insulin with poor intake in ESRD is a classic seizure cause, but glucose is 142

differential.diagnosis: Drug accumulation seizure (for example cefepime) in ESRD
differential.key_features: No renally cleared neurotoxic drug on his list
Temperature 37.4 C, WBC 12.8 after a convulsion, no infective source

key_clinical_evidence: Missed dialysis with BUN 142, calcium 6.8, sodium 128 and acidosis is a layered seizure precipitant; potassium 6.8 adds the cardiac emergency
Emergency hemodialysis is the definitive treatment, gently at first to avoid disequilibrium
Antiseizure maintenance doses need renal adjustment in ESRD; loading doses do not
Uremic platelet dysfunction increases SDH risk: CT first

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Brown is a 61-year-old African American man with ESRD on hemodialysis who is brought by ambulance in active status epilepticus after his wife called 911. She reports he missed his scheduled Monday dialysis session yesterday due to transportation issues; his last dialysis was on Friday, 4 days ago, and it is now Tuesday. He had been feeling increasingly confused and nauseated over the past 24 hours and ate little, although he took his usual insulin. He developed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure approximately 20 minutes ago that has not stopped. He has no prior history of seizures or epilepsy. His wife reports he drank significantly more fluids than usual yesterday because he felt thirsty.
